analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal office that would manufacture affordable generic drugs, including insulin, and sell them at a fair price.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past referral: one sponsor, no cosponsors, and no committee action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. That office would make prescription drugs when prices are high, competition is thin, or shortages hit, starting with insulin, and sell them at a price set to keep them accessible. It would also make key drug ingredients to help generic companies enter the market. The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 115th Congress, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay out of pocket for expensive generics or insulin, and taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid, gain a government-run manufacturer that competes on price in markets with few makers or rising prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing high drug and insulin prices

how_it_helps.text: The office would manufacture drugs when three or fewer companies sell them, prices have risen faster than medical inflation, the drug is on the shortage list, or its price blocks access to a World Health Organization essential medicine [S3].
Within one year the office would have to begin public manufacturing of insulin, and to be producing at least 15 drugs within one year and 25 within three years [S3].
The office would set a fair price considering patient access, program costs, and manufacturing costs, and would sell to other entities at that price [S3].
It would manufacture scarce active ingredients when needed to help new generic manufacturers enter the market [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and other drug manufacturers face a new public competitor on drugs whose patents have expired, and the federal government pays to build and run the manufacturing operation out of appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Building a government drug manufacturer is a costly, open-ended commitment: the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate, and drug manufacturing carries real compliance, quality, and recall risks [S3].

The bill's coverage is narrow: it applies only to drugs whose patents and exclusivity have expired or that qualify under federal march-in and licensing authorities, so it would not lower prices on drugs still under patent [S3].

A public manufacturer selling at a set fair price would compete directly with private generic companies, and a subsidy-backed competitor could squeeze them even as its ingredient program helps some of them enter the market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who depend on insulin or scarce, high-priced generics, a public manufacturer is a direct, structural answer to prices and shortages. The tradeoff is real: it costs taxpayers an open-ended amount, reaches only off-patent drugs, and puts government in competition with the generic industry. No hearing or estimate was ever produced, so the design was never tested in public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: introduced December 19, 2018, referred to Energy and Commerce the same day, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before Congress ended two weeks later [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Affordable Drug Manufacturing Act of 2018 on December 19, 2018 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
No further action of any kind was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers keep markets without a public competitor, and taxpayers avoid the cost of building one; patients facing high insulin and generic prices gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would create a federal drug-manufacturing office; it was her only recorded action on it before Congress ended

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on December 19, 2018 and took no further action on it before the Congress ended; no hearing or markup was scheduled

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without action for the remaining two weeks of the 115th Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so no record exists of where the chambers stood [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill creates a public manufacturer that competes on off-patent drugs where few makers charge high prices, and it can acquire rights to manufacture through federal licensing and march-in authorities. Manufacturers currently earn monopoly prices in exactly those thin-competition markets the office would target [S3].

The office would compete directly with generics by selling approved drugs at a set fair price, but it would also manufacture scarce active ingredients to help new generic makers enter the market. The industry's interest in cheaper ingredients runs with patients'; its interest in exclusive markets does not [S3].

The bill bans former registered drug manufacturer lobbyists and former senior executives of drug companies under federal enforcement actions from running or working in the new office for six years, closing a revolving door into the program it creates [S3].
